title: Civil Rights era, wearing blinders, and no regrets
summary: He says jazz would have evolved regardless of politics, he was obsessed with belonging, and he would do it all again, citing Art Blakey.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: It just occurred to me that 1964 is a significant year for you, it was also the Civil Rights Bill of 1964, and if you extrapolate on that, was the situation socially and politically at that time, do you feel it affected the change in jazz that you’re describing?

Well I think that the development of the jazz art form would have happened the way it did even if the social and political developments didn’t happen around that same time. But of course a lot of the artists, they delved into that, you know, with the music, you know, Charles Mingus and others, Max Roach you know. But honestly, although I was paying close attention to what was going on socially and politically, I didn’t write or play my music with that in mind. Now it might be hard for folks to believe that didn’t have that kind of effect on me. But I sort of had blinders on you know. As I said, initially, once I realized I could do something with this art form, I just wanted to belong. And in order for me to accomplish that I put blinders on basically to everything else you know.
Is it safe to say you were obsessed with it?
I was totally obsessed with it, ‘til now.
Well it makes me wonder, I was sort of going to ask this question wherever our interview wraps up, but I’ll try it now. Do you feel that you have sacrificed or given anything up for this music?

Absolutely not. If I had it to do all over again I’d do exactly the same. Every bit of it you know. I mean we are blessed in a way, you know, us artisans I mean and it doesn’t matter which idiom it is: jazz music, classical music, popular music, minimalist, you know. Because Art Blakey’s well-said powerful in that inimitable voice of his, you know, when he would get off the drums and speak to the audience and said, “We’re here to wash away the dust of your everyday life.” And so I carry that in mind you know. And so —
